messages.content: A campus IT help desk gets walk-ins at about 6.2 per hour and one technician resolves them at about 8 per hour on average. Assuming arrivals are Poisson and service times exponential, what is the average total time a student spends in the system, and the average time spent waiting before service starts?

With one technician this is an M/M/1 queue: utilization is 6.2/8 = 0.775, busy but stable. The mean time in the system is W = 1/(8 − 6.2) = 0.556 hours, about 0.6 in hours or roughly 33 minutes door to door. The mean wait before service starts is Wq = λ/(μ(μ − λ)) = 0.431 hours, about 26 minutes, so most of the visit is queue, not repair. The assumption doing the work is the exponential service time: if real repairs are more uniform than exponential, the true wait is shorter; if a few repairs balloon, it is longer. At 77.5% utilization the queue is also sensitive — a 10% arrival bump would push waits up far more than 10%.

A coffee drive-thru serves 22 cars per hour with one window, and cars arrive at 18 per hour in the morning peak. How many cars are in the system on average, and how many of those are waiting in line rather than at the window?

Little's law on an M/M/1 gives L = λ/(μ − λ) = 4.50 cars in the system on average, and Lq = λ²/(μ(μ − λ)) = 3.68 of them are waiting in line while the remaining ~1 car is at the window being served. Utilization is 18/22 ≈ 0.82, which is why a four-car average line forms even though the window is idle 18% of the time: arrivals bunch randomly, and the queue drains only at the 4-per-hour spare capacity. These are long-run averages under Poisson arrivals and exponential service; a real peak that ramps up and down within the hour will show a worse worst-case line than the average suggests.

An airport security lane processes 145 passengers per hour and passengers arrive at 132 per hour during the morning bank. What is the probability an arriving passenger has to wait at all, and what is the probability the total time in the lane exceeds 10 minutes?

In an M/M/1 an arrival waits whenever the server is busy, which happens with probability ρ = 0.910 — over 90% of passengers queue at least briefly. The total time in system is exponential with rate μ − λ = 13 per hour, so P(T > 10 min) = exp(−13 × 1/6) = 0.115: about an 11% chance of exceeding ten minutes even though the mean time is only 60/13 ≈ 4.6 minutes. (The related queue-only tail, P(wait > 10 min before service starts), is ρ × exp(−13/6) = 0.104.) That gap between a comfortable mean and a fat tail is the operational lesson: staffing to the average still leaves one passenger in ten with a slow trip through the lane. The model assumes a single exponential server; a lane that meters passengers in batches behaves differently.

A small clinic's check-in desk sees 9 patients per hour and the receptionist completes check-in at 12 per hour. Use Little's law to find the average number of patients in the check-in process and the average check-in time.

Little's law says L = λW, and for this single-desk M/M/1, W = 1/(μ − λ) = 0.333 hours, exactly 20 minutes from joining the process to being checked in. The average number in the process is L = 3.0 patients — typically two waiting and one at the desk. Little's law itself needs no distributional assumption, only a stable system where everyone eventually leaves; the 20-minute figure does lean on the Poisson/exponential model. If arrivals come in appointment-driven waves rather than randomly, the same averages can hide a predictable 9 a.m. pile-up that the steady-state number smooths away.

A web API receives 340 requests per minute and a single worker instance handles 400 per minute. The team wants the probability that an arriving request finds 5 or more requests already in the system. Compute it under M/M/1 assumptions.

For an M/M/1 in steady state, P(N ≥ k) = ρ^k with ρ = 340/400 = 0.85, so P(N ≥ 5) = 0.85^5 = 0.444 — roughly 44% of arriving requests find five or more already in the system. That sounds alarming until you note the mean system size is ρ/(1 − ρ) ≈ 5.7: at 85% utilization a five-deep system is the normal state, not an anomaly. The actionable number is the tail's sensitivity: adding a second worker does not just halve this probability, it collapses it, because the spare capacity grows from 60 to 460 requests per minute. The geometric tail is an M/M/1 artifact; heavy-tailed service times would fatten it further.

Explain why a call center staffed to exactly 100% of average demand will see its queue grow without bound, using a concrete example with calls arriving at 30 per hour and agents handling 30 per hour in total.

Because a queue has no memory of the good minutes. If calls arrive at 30 per hour and the team can serve exactly 30 per hour, utilization is 1.00 — every agent busy all the time. In any given ten minutes, randomness delivers 7 calls instead of the average 5; the extra 2 wait. The next ten minutes deliver exactly 5, but there is no idle capacity to work off the backlog, because the agents are still fully occupied with new arrivals. Each unlucky burst adds a permanent layer to the queue, and lucky bursts never remove one, since spare capacity is zero. Formally the system has no steady state at ρ = 1: the expected queue length grows like the square root of elapsed time, forever. Real centers therefore staff to 85–92% utilization, buying drain capacity with planned idleness.

A pharmacy counter has one pharmacist filling 14 prescriptions per hour while orders arrive at 11 per hour. What fraction of orders wait longer than 15 minutes in the queue (not counting fill time), under M/M/1 assumptions?

For M/M/1, the queue wait tail is P(Wq > t) = ρ·exp(−(μ − λ)t). With ρ = 11/14 ≈ 0.786 and μ − λ = 3 per hour, P(Wq > 0.25 h) = 0.371 — about 37% of orders wait over fifteen minutes before filling even starts, despite a mean queue wait of only λ/(μ(μ−λ)) ≈ 15.7 minutes and an idle pharmacist 21% of the time. The mean and the tail tell different stories because the wait distribution is a mixture: 21% of orders wait zero, and the rest draw from an exponential with a long right tail. If the pharmacy quotes a 20-minute pickup promise, this tail — not the mean — is the number that decides how often the promise breaks.

A support chat team is choosing between one fast agent handling 20 chats/hour and two agents each handling 11 chats/hour, with chats arriving at 16/hour. Using M/M/1 for the first option and the M/M/2 Erlang-C approximation via the pooled-server comparison, which gives the lower mean wait in queue? Work the M/M/1 exactly and the M/M/2 with the Erlang C formula.

Option one, the single fast agent, is an M/M/1 with Wq = 0.200 hours, exactly 12 minutes. For two slower agents the offered load is a = 1.45 erlangs; the Erlang C probability that an arrival waits is 0.612, and Wq = C/(cμ − λ) = 0.102 hours, about 6.1 minutes. Two slower agents win on wait — partly because their combined capacity is actually higher (22 vs 20 per hour), and partly because of pooling: a chat is never stuck behind one long conversation while another agent sits idle. Pooling beats raw speed here because the second server absorbs variance. Caveat: Erlang C assumes exponential service and no abandonment; real chat agents handling three concurrent chats break both assumptions.

A toll plaza lane passes 500 vehicles per hour at capacity and traffic arrives at 460 per hour in the evening peak. How long is the average delay per vehicle, and what happens to that delay if arrivals rise just 5%?

Modeled as M/M/1, the mean queue delay at 460 arrivals/hour is Wq = 0.02300 hours — about 1.4 minutes per vehicle, noticeable but tolerable. Raise arrivals 5% to 483/hour and spare capacity falls from 40 to 17 vehicles/hour; delay becomes 0.05682 hours, about 3.4 minutes — a 147% increase in delay from a 5% increase in demand. That nonlinearity is the whole story of congestion near capacity: delay scales with 1/(μ − λ), so as the gap closes the delay explodes. The practical implication is that the last few percent of capacity are worth far more than the first few, and a small toll-price nudge at peak buys outsized relief. Real platoons from traffic lights violate the Poisson assumption and make peaks lumpier still.

A bakery's single oven line finishes a batch every 6 minutes on average, and orders needing the oven arrive at 7 per hour. What is the oven's utilization and the average number of orders in the oven system?

Six minutes per batch is a service rate of 10 per hour, so utilization ρ = 0.70 — the oven is productively busy 70% of the time. The mean number of orders in the system is L = λ/(μ − λ) = 2.33: on average a bit over two orders are somewhere in the oven pipeline, one baking and roughly 1.3 waiting for a slot. At 70% utilization the system still has slack to absorb a catering order without a crisis, which is exactly the headroom the owner wants before committing to a standing wholesale account. If that account adds 2 orders/hour, ρ rises to 0.9 and L jumps to 9 — the same oven, a completely different operation.

A manager says: 'Our average wait is only 4 minutes, so customers are fine.' The wait distribution is exponential with that mean. What share of customers wait more than 10 minutes, and why does the mean mislead here?

For an exponential distribution the tail is P(W > t) = exp(−t/mean), so P(W > 10) = exp(−2.5) = 0.082 — about 8% of customers, one in twelve, wait more than ten minutes while the 'average' customer waits four. The mean misleads because the exponential is right-skewed: its median is only 4 × ln 2 ≈ 2.8 minutes, and a long thin tail of badly-served customers pulls the mean up while remaining individually miserable. Customers also remember and review their worst waits, not the average. Operationally the fix is to manage a percentile — '90% served within 8 minutes' — because percentile targets force attention onto the tail where dissatisfaction actually lives. If waits were instead tightly clustered around 4 minutes (say, appointment-based), the same mean would be perfectly reassuring; the distribution shape, not the mean, carries the risk.

A municipal permit office has arrivals of 4.5 per hour and one clerk processing 6 per hour. A consultant proposes a second clerk. First quantify the current mean total time in the office per applicant.

Today an applicant spends W = 1/(μ − λ) = 0.667 hours — 40 minutes — in the office on average, of which Wq = 0.500 hours (30 minutes) is pure waiting and 10 minutes is the service itself. Utilization is 75%, which sounds slack, yet the wait is triple the service time; that ratio, λ/(μ − λ) scaled, is what applicants actually feel. A second clerk would cut the wait dramatically (an M/M/2 at this load waits only a few minutes), but the honest framing for the budget meeting is cost per applicant-minute saved, and whether the 30-minute wait is a real harm or merely an annoyance. The M/M/1 numbers assume walk-in randomness; if most applicants arrive at 9 a.m. when doors open, the lived wait is worse than the steady-state figure.

An email support inbox receives 85 tickets per day and the team resolves 100 per day. Tickets that sit are worked oldest-first. Under an M/M/1 approximation, what is the mean age of a ticket when work starts on it, and the probability a ticket waits more than one full day before work starts?

Treating the inbox as a queue with λ = 85 and μ = 100 per day, the mean wait before work starts is Wq = 0.0567 days — about 1.4 working hours, fine on average. The tail is the problem: P(Wq > 1 day) = ρ·exp(−(μ − λ)·1) = 0.000000, essentially zero — wait, that result exposes the model's weakness rather than the inbox's health. Real ticket queues breach day-old waits constantly because arrivals arrive in Monday-morning bursts and service is not exponential; the M/M/1 tail decays at rate (μ − λ) = 15/day, far faster than real backlogs clear. The right use of this computation is as a lower bound and a diagnostic: if the real day-old fraction is much larger than 0.0000, the gap measures how non-Poisson the arrival pattern is, which points at staffing-by-hour rather than staffing-by-day as the fix.

A gym has one squat rack. Members arrive wanting it at 5 per hour during peak and a session averages 9 minutes. What is the probability the rack is free when a member walks up, and the mean wait for it?

Nine-minute sessions give a service rate of 60/9 ≈ 6.67 per hour, so utilization is 5/6.67 = 0.75 and the rack stands free 0.25 of the time — one walk-up in four finds it open. The rest wait Wq = 0.450 hours on average, about 27 minutes, which at gym scale is effectively 'not available this workout' and explains why members route around it. The queueing insight for the manager is that a second rack does not halve the problem, it nearly erases it: two racks at this load run at 37.5% utilization each in a pooled system where waits collapse to a couple of minutes. The exponential-session assumption is shaky — real sessions cluster at programmed lengths — but the utilization arithmetic, which needs no such assumption, already makes the case.
A single mechanic completes inspections at 3 per hour; cars arrive at 2.1 per hour. Find the average number of cars at the shop and the average time a car spends there.

With λ = 2.1 and μ = 3 per hour, the average number of cars at the shop is L = λ/(μ − λ) = 2.33, and each car spends W = 1/(μ − λ) = 1.111 hours there — about 67 minutes, of which 20 minutes is the inspection itself and roughly 47 is waiting for the lift. Utilization is 70%, a healthy target for a one-mechanic shop: busy enough to pay, slack enough that a walk-in does not wreck the schedule. The owner should watch the arrival rate, not the average: if a fleet contract pushes arrivals to 2.7/hour, utilization hits 90% and the average stay balloons to over three hours, at which point a second mechanic stops being a luxury. Averages here are steady-state; the first car of the day never waits at all.

A data pipeline's single consumer processes 950 messages per second while producers send 900 per second. The team alerts when backlog exceeds 10,000 messages. Under M/M/1, what is the probability the backlog (messages in system) is at or above 50, and what mean drain time applies to a burst of 10,000 extra messages?

The steady-state system size is geometric: P(N ≥ 50) = ρ^50 = 0.067 — about a 6.7% chance at any random instant of seeing 50+ messages in flight, with a mean system size of ρ/(1−ρ) = 18. The burst question is different and more useful: a 10,000-message burst drains only at the spare rate μ − λ = 50/second, taking 200 seconds — over three minutes — during which the consumer is saturated and latency for everything behind the burst is elevated. Teams routinely under-size this: the steady-state numbers look tiny while the recovery time from one deploy hiccup is minutes. The geometric tail assumes exponential service; a consumer with occasional 10-second GC pauses has a materially fatter backlog tail than this model admits.

Two otherwise identical clinics differ only in variability: Clinic A books appointments evenly, Clinic B takes only walk-ins. Both run at 85% utilization with the same mean service time of 10 minutes. Using the Kingman approximation intuition, explain which waits longer and by roughly what factor if B's service-and-arrival variability factor is about 2.4 times A's.

Clinic B waits longer, by roughly the variability ratio itself. The Kingman approximation says the mean queue wait is proportional to ρ/(1−ρ) × (mean service time) × a variability factor (ca² + cs²)/2 built from the squared coefficients of variation of arrivals and service. Both clinics share ρ/(1−ρ) ≈ 5.67 and the same 10-minute service, so the wait ratio is just the variability ratio: B's mean wait is about 2.4 times A's. Scheduled arrivals push ca² toward 0 (arrivals are nearly deterministic), while walk-ins are Poisson (ca² ≈ 1) and unscheduled service surprises push cs² up too. This is why appointment systems feel calmer at identical utilization, and why 'we're only at 85%' is no defense for a walk-in operation: at high utilization, variability is not noise around the wait — it is the wait's main ingredient.

A bakery sells sourdough at $9 with a unit cost of $3.40; unsold loaves are day-old discounted, recovering $1.20. Daily demand averages 84 loaves. Using the newsvendor critical fractile, what in-stock probability should the bake quantity target?

The underage cost of one loaf too few is the lost margin Cu = 9 − 3.40 = $5.60; the overage cost of one too many is Co = 3.40 − 1.20 = $2.20. The critical fractile is Cu/(Cu + Co) = 0.718 — the bakery should bake the 71.8th percentile of daily demand, not the mean of 84. Baking the mean would stock out on roughly half of all days, which is far too often when a stockout costs 2.5 times what an overage costs. The fractile says nothing about the quantity until it is mapped through the demand distribution: with a standard deviation of, say, 12 loaves, the target is roughly 84 + 0.58×12 ≈ 91 loaves. The assumption to name: each day is independent and unsold value really is $1.20 — if day-old loaves cannibalize fresh sales, the true salvage is lower and the target drops.

A parts distributor faces weekly demand with mean 240 and standard deviation 38 for a filter cartridge; replenishment lead time is 2 weeks and demand weeks are independent. For a 97.5% cycle service level (z = 1.96), compute the safety stock and reorder point.

Demand over the 2-week lead time has mean 480 and, with independent weeks, standard deviation 38√2 = 53.7. Safety stock at z = 1.96 is 105.3, about 105 units, and the reorder point is 480 + 105 = 585 units. The √2 is doing quiet work: risk pools over time, so doubling lead time raises the buffer by 41%, not 100%. The independence assumption is the fragile one — if a promotion or a fleet customer's outage makes the two weeks' demand move together, the true lead-time spread is larger and 105 units buys less than 97.5% service. Cycle service level also deserves honesty: 97.5% means 1 cycle in 40 stocks out, not that 97.5% of units demanded are filled.

An online retailer stocks a phone case with daily demand mean 130, sd 26, and a 4-day lead time. They currently hold 90 units of safety stock. What cycle service level are they actually running, and what stockout probability per cycle does that imply?

Lead-time demand has standard deviation 26√4 = 52, so 90 units of safety stock is z = 1.73 standard deviations of cover. That corresponds to a cycle service level of Φ(1.73) = 0.958 — about 95.8% — and a stockout probability of 0.042, roughly 1 cycle in 24. Whether that is good depends on the margin math, not on the roundness of 95%: for a low-margin commodity case it may be generous; for a case that anchors a bundle sale it may be cheap insurance. The normal model also flatters the tail here — daily demand for a single SKU is usually right-skewed and promotion-driven, so the true stockout rate is probably somewhat worse than 4.2%. Measuring actual cycle outcomes for a quarter beats trusting the curve.

A grocery orders milk with a 1-day lead time. Daily demand averages 210 gallons with sd 30. If the store wants at most a 5% chance of running out before the next delivery, how much safety stock above mean daily demand is needed (z for 95% = 1.645)?

With a one-day lead time there is no time-pooling: lead-time demand is just one day's demand, mean 210, sd 30. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 1.645 × 30 = 49.4 gallons, so the store should have about 259 gallons positioned at order time. The honest caveat is that milk demand is not normal at the edges — a heat wave or a school-holiday week shifts the whole distribution, and no z-value protects against a mean that moved. The 5% target also deserves a sanity check against spoilage: milk unsold is a write-off, so the newsvendor trade-off (stockout cost vs waste cost), not a blanket service target, should set this number. For a staple that drives store trips, though, the stockout cost includes the basket the shopper takes elsewhere, which argues for the generous buffer.

A warehouse uses a reorder point of 640 units. Mean lead-time demand is 560 with sd 55. A manager claims this gives 'about 93% service.' Verify the claim and find the reorder point needed for 98% (z = 2.054).

The current buffer is 80 units, z = 1.45, giving Φ(1.45) = 0.927 — about 92.7%, so the manager's 'about 93%' checks out. Moving to 98% requires a reorder point of 673 units, i.e. safety stock rising from 80 to about 113 units. Note the price of the last few points: going from 93% to 98% cuts stockouts by more than two-thirds but costs 41% more buffer stock, and the next two points to 99.9% would cost far more again. Service-level decisions are really decisions about which stockouts you are buying your way out of. The calculation assumes lead-time demand is normal with a stable sd of 55; if that sd was estimated in a quiet quarter, both service figures are optimistic.

Explain the difference between cycle service level and fill rate, with a concrete example: 20 replenishment cycles a year, one cycle stocks out and loses 40 units of demand out of 12,000 units demanded annually.

They answer different questions. Cycle service level asks 'in what fraction of cycles did we never stock out?' — here 0.95, 95%, because one of twenty cycles ran dry. Fill rate asks 'what fraction of demand was met from stock?' — here 1 − 40/12,000 = 0.9967, 99.67%, because the single stockout was shallow. A company can honestly report a 99.7% fill rate while one customer in twenty orders hits an empty shelf, and both numbers are 'the service level' in somebody's slide deck. Fill rate is usually the better customer proxy, but it hides concentration: if the 40 lost units were all one key account's order, the average is a lie where it matters. When a supplier quotes a service figure, the first question is always which of these two it is, and the second is over what window it was measured.

A fashion retailer buys a seasonal jacket at $46 and sells at $110; leftovers go to clearance at $28. Demand is forecast normal with mean 1,900 and sd 420. Find the critical fractile and the optimal order quantity (use z = 0.93 for the fractile).

Underage cost Cu = 110 − 46 = $64 of lost margin per jacket short; overage cost Co = 46 − 28 = $18 lost per leftover. The critical fractile is 0.780, the 78th percentile of demand — high, because a stockout hurts 3.6 times as much as a leftover. Mapping through the forecast, Q* = 1,900 + 0.93 × 420 = 2291 jackets, roughly 2,291. Ordering the mean (1,900) would be the classic error: it balances units, not money. Two assumptions deserve naming. First, the normal forecast for a fashion item is a polite fiction — real seasonal demand is often bimodal (hit or flop), which pushes the optimal quantity around depending on which mode the buyer believes. Second, clearance at $28 assumes the clearance channel absorbs any volume at that price; a flop year floods it and the true salvage falls, which would lower Q*.

A supplier's lead time varies: mean 6 days, sd 1.5 days. Daily demand averages 48 units with sd 9, independent of lead time. Compute the standard deviation of lead-time demand and the safety stock for 95% service (z = 1.645).

When lead time itself is random, lead-time demand variance has two parts: mean lead time × daily variance, plus mean daily demand² × lead-time variance: 6×81 + 48²×2.25 = 486 + 5,184, so the standard deviation is 75.3 units. Safety stock at 95% is 124 units — and the decomposition is the insight: 5,184 of the 5,670 variance (over 91%) comes from lead-time variability, not demand variability. The cheapest service improvement here is not more stock or better forecasting; it is a more reliable supplier, because every day of lead-time sd removed cuts the buffer quadratically. Teams that model lead time as fixed at its mean would compute a safety stock near 36 units and then wonder why stockouts keep happening.

A bike shop keeps 14 spare tubes as safety stock. Daily demand for tubes averages 6 with sd 2.5, lead time is 2 days with independent days. What stockout probability per replenishment cycle does the current safety stock imply?

Lead-time demand sd is 2.5√2 = 3.54, so 14 tubes of safety stock is z = 3.96 — nearly four standard deviations of cover. The implied stockout probability per cycle is 0.000038, effectively zero under the normal model; the shop is carrying far more buffer than demand randomness justifies. That said, the normal model is thinnest exactly here: tube demand arrives in lumps (one rider replaces both tires, a weekend group ride wipes the shelf), so a small deliberate over-buffer is defensible. Still, 14 tubes ties up cash and shelf space against a risk the math prices at nearly nil; 8 tubes would still give z ≈ 2.3, about a 1% cycle stockout rate. The real exposure is a supplier delay, which safety stock sized on demand variance does not address at all.

A critical spare part for a bottling line: stocking out costs an estimated $38,000 per day of downtime and the line consumes the part on failure only, averaging 3.1 failures per year. Holding one spare costs $2,900 per year. The number of failures per year is Poisson. Compare the expected annual cost of stocking zero spares versus one spare (with one spare, a stockout needs 2+ failures before replenishment, assume instant replenishment after the first failure is impossible — instead, with one spare the line is down only if a second failure occurs within the 30-day replenishment window; failure rate during window = 3.1 × 30/365).

This is an expected-value comparison, and the honest answer needs the model stated plainly. With no spare, each of the 3.1 failures per year idles the line until the part arrives; even a single day of downtime per event at $38,000 dwarfs the holding cost, so zero spares loses immediately. With one spare, the line only goes down if a second failure lands inside the 30-day replenishment window. The expected failure count in a window is λw = 0.255; the chance of at least one second failure in a given window is 0.225, and across 3.1 windows a year the expected number of downtime events falls to 0.697 per year. Against a $2,900 holding cost, one spare is overwhelmingly worth it — the break-even would need downtime valued under roughly a hundred dollars a day. The model's soft spots: failures may cluster (a failing part can signal a degrading line, violating Poisson independence), and the 30-day window is itself a supplier promise, not a constant.

Daily demand for a snack bar at a gym is Poisson with mean 46. The gym stocks 55 bars each morning. What is the probability of selling out today (use a normal approximation with continuity correction)?

For a Poisson, the standard deviation is √46 = 6.78. Stocking 55 means selling out requires demand of 56+, which with the continuity correction is z = 1.40. The sell-out probability is about 0.081 — roughly 8%, or two days a month. The manager's real question is whether 8% is right, and that is a newsvendor question in disguise: bars are cheap, margins decent, and a sold-out customer often substitutes another product, so the true underage cost is small and 8% may be fine. If instead the empty shelf sends members to the café next door, the underage cost includes the whole basket and the stock target should rise. The normal approximation is respectable at mean 46; for a slow item with mean demand of 3 it would mislead and the exact Poisson tail should be used.

A retailer says 'we stock the forecast' for a product with symmetric forecast error and equal costs either way, then asks why they still stock out half the time. Explain, and compute the expected units short per cycle if demand is normal with mean 500, sd 60, stocked at 500 (expected shortage for z=0 is sd × 0.3989).

Stocking the mean of a symmetric distribution means demand exceeds stock with probability one half — stocking out half the time is not bad luck, it is the arithmetic of the decision. The mean is a balance point of probability, not a service target. The expected shortage per cycle at z = 0 is σ × L(0) = 23.9 units: on average about 24 units of demand go unmet each cycle, concentrated in the bad half of cycles where the shortfall averages about 48. The fix is not a better forecast — even a perfect forecaster of the mean faces the same coin flip. The fix is choosing a service target from costs: the newsvendor fractile weighs the margin lost on a stockout against the cost of an unsold unit, and only when those are exactly equal does stocking the mean happen to be right. 'We stock the forecast' quietly assumes that equality, usually without anyone having checked it.

Two warehouses pool safety stock for the same part. Separately, each faces lead-time demand sd of 85 and holds z = 1.645 safety stock. If their demands are independent, what is the pooled safety stock for the same service level, and the percentage saving? What if demand correlation is 0.6?

Separately the two sites hold 280 units of safety stock in total (140 each). Pooled, with independent demands, the combined sd is 85√2 and the pooled safety stock is 198 — a saving of 29.3%, the classic square-root law: risk pooling cuts buffers by 1 − 1/√n. With correlation 0.6 between the sites' demands, the pooled safety stock rises to 250 units and the saving shrinks to about 11%. Correlation is the silent killer of pooling business cases: regional demand for weather-driven parts moves together, so the pooled buffer converges back toward the un-pooled one. Before promising the √n saving, estimate the correlation from overlapping history — and remember pooling also adds transshipment time, which eats part of the gain in practice.

A distributor's fill rate target is 98%. In the last quarter they shipped 1,240,000 units and backordered 31,500 units. Did they hit the target, and how many fewer backordered units would have been needed?

The actual fill rate is 1 − 31,500/1,240,000 = 0.9746 — 97.46%, so no, they missed the 98% target. At 98%, allowable backorders were 24800 units; they exceeded that by 6700 units, about 6,700 units of demand that waited or walked. Framing matters for the review meeting: the miss is 0.54 percentage points of fill rate, but it is 27% more backorders than the target permits — the same fact, and the second framing is the one that reflects customer experience. Averages also conceal where the backorders sat: if they concentrated in a few SKUs or one large account, the aggregate 97.46% understates the damage. The corrective lever (more safety stock on the offending SKUs versus expediting) should be chosen from that concentration data, not from the headline rate.

A coffee shop goes through espresso beans with daily usage mean 8 kg, sd 1.6 kg. The supplier delivers 3 days after ordering. The owner orders when 30 kg remain. Is that reorder point sensible if she wants roughly a 2.5% stockout risk per cycle (z = 1.96)?

Mean lead-time demand is 24 kg with sd 2.77 kg. A 2.5% stockout risk needs a reorder point of 29.4 kg, call it 29.4. Her 30 kg trigger implies z = 2.17, about a 1.5% cycle stockout risk — slightly more conservative than her stated target, and sensibly so: the difference is 0.6 kg of beans, trivial money, while a stockout means no espresso drinks at all, the shop's core product. This is the general pattern for cheap, critical inputs: the cost asymmetry argues for buffers that look excessive on a spreadsheet. The assumption to watch is the 3-day delivery: if the supplier occasionally takes 5 days, lead-time variability, which this calculation ignores, becomes the dominant risk and the reorder point should be set from the delivery distribution, not the usage one.

An electronics retailer must order a game console bundle before launch. Cost $310, price $449, unsold units can be returned for a $265 credit. Expected demand mean 640, sd 150. Compute the critical fractile and optimal order (z at fractile ≈ 0.44).

Cu = 449 − 310 = $139; Co = 310 − 265 = $45. The critical fractile is 0.755 — order the 75.5th percentile of demand. With the normal forecast, Q* = 640 + 0.44 × 150 = 706 units. The return credit is what makes ordering deep rational: it caps the downside per unit at $45 while the upside is $139, a 3-to-1 asymmetry. Two cautions before signing the PO. First, launch demand forecasts are not really normal — they are mixtures of 'hit' and 'meh' scenarios, and if the buyer privately believes the flop scenario is likely, the fractile should be applied to that mixture, not the smooth curve. Second, return credits usually come with freight and handling strings and a return window; if returning 200 units costs $12 each in freight, Co rises to $57 and the optimal quantity falls by roughly 25 units. Small print moves optimal orders.

Build a small decision table for a produce distributor choosing safety stock for avocados: lead-time demand mean 900 crates, sd 120. Compare safety stock 0, 100, 200, 300 on implied z, cycle service level, and expected units short per cycle (use loss-function values L(z): L(0)=0.3989, L(0.83)=0.1173, L(1.67)=0.0199, L(2.5)=0.0020). Present it as a table with a recommendation.

Expected shortage per cycle is σ × L(z), and service level is Φ(z):

| Safety stock | z | Cycle service | Expected short (crates) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.00 | 50.0% | 47.9 |
| 100 | 0.83 | 79.7% | 14.1 |
| 200 | 1.67 | 95.2% | 2.4 |
| 300 | 2.50 | 99.4% | 0.24 |

The diminishing returns are stark: the first 100 crates of buffer cut expected shortages by about 34 crates per cycle; the third 100 crates buy only about 2. For a perishable like avocados, where unsold buffer is tomorrow's spoilage, the middle row is usually the economic answer — but the table's job is to make the trade visible, not to pick the row. If a shortage means losing a supermarket contract, row four is cheap; if it means a spot-market scramble at a modest premium, row two wins. The loss-function values assume normal lead-time demand; avocado demand spikes around promotions and holidays, so treat the right-hand column as a floor on true shortages.

An A/B test: control converted 1,240 of 12,000 visitors (10.33%), variant converted 1,372 of 12,100 (11.34%). Compute the difference, its standard error, the z-statistic, and a 95% confidence interval for the true difference.

The observed lift is 0.0101 — about 1.0 percentage point — with standard error 0.0040, giving z = 2.51, past the 1.96 line. The 95% confidence interval runs from 0.0022 to 0.0179: the data are consistent with a true effect anywhere from roughly +0.2 to +1.8 percentage points. That range, not the z-score, is the decision input: even the pessimistic end is positive here, so shipping is defensible, but a business case built on the point estimate (+1.0) should be stress-tested at +0.2. The interval assumes independent visitors and no peeking-driven early stop; if the team checked daily and stopped when it 'looked significant,' the true interval is wider than this one.

Before running a pricing-page test, a team wants 80% power at 5% significance (two-sided) to detect a lift from 4.0% to 4.6% conversion. How many visitors per group are required? Use z values 1.96 and 0.84.

The per-group sample size is n = (1.96 + 0.84)² × [p₁(1−p₁) + p₂(1−p₂)] / Δ² = 17920 visitors per group — roughly 17,900, or about 36,000 total. The number shocks teams because the effect is small relative to the noise: a 0.6-point lift on a 4% base is a 15% relative improvement, yet each visitor contributes only a Bernoulli coin flip of information. The levers are unforgiving: halving the detectable effect quadruples the required n, and running at 90% power instead of 80% adds about a third more. If the page only gets 2,000 visitors a week, this test needs nine weeks — which forces the real conversation: either accept detection of only larger effects, test on a higher-traffic surface, or decide the pricing question another way. Power calculations done after the test, using the observed effect, are meaningless; this one is honest because the 0.6 points came from the business threshold, not the data.

A test reads: variant revenue per visitor $4.82 (sd $21.40, n = 8,400), control $4.55 (sd $20.90, n = 8,350). Compute the standard error of the difference in means and the 95% CI. Is the revenue lift established?

The difference is $0.27 per visitor with standard error 0.327, so the 95% interval is (-0.371, 0.911) — it comfortably includes zero and negative values down to about −$0.37. The revenue lift is not established; the point estimate is a coin flip dressed as a gain. Revenue per visitor is the hardest common metric to move because its standard deviation ($21) dwarfs its mean ($4.70): a handful of whale orders dominate. With this variance, detecting a true $0.27 lift would need roughly four times the sample. Practical options: run longer, cap or winsorize extreme orders (decided in advance), or judge the test on the conversion metric it was powered for and treat revenue as directional only. What not to do is report '+5.9% revenue' without the interval — that is how organizations ship noise.

A stakeholder asks why the team won't just stop the test 'as soon as it's significant.' Explain the peeking problem quantitatively: if you check a true null test 10 times at the 5% level, roughly what is the chance of at least one false 'significant' reading (use the independent-check approximation, then qualify it)?

Each peek at a null test has a 5% chance of crossing the line by luck. Peek 10 times and, if the checks were independent, the chance of at least one false alarm is 1 − 0.95^10 = 0.401 — about 40%. Successive peeks at accumulating data are not independent (they share most of their data), so the true inflation is less than 40% but still lands around 15–20% for ten looks — three to four times the advertised error rate. The intuition: a random walk of the z-statistic wanders, and given enough looks it will eventually touch any fixed boundary even when nothing is there. This is not pedantry; it systematically manufactures false wins, and because teams stop on wins but never on losses, the shipped 'wins' regress to nothing and trust in the testing program dies. The legitimate escapes are pre-registered fixed horizons, sequential methods with alpha-spending (which budget the error across looks), or Bayesian decision rules stated in advance. 'We stopped when it looked good' is none of those.
A landing page converts 312 of 4,800 visitors. Give the 95% confidence interval for the true conversion rate using the normal approximation.

The observed rate is 0.0650 (6.50%) with standard error 0.0036, so the 95% interval is (0.0580, 0.0720) — the true rate is plausibly anywhere from about 5.8% to 7.2%. That ±0.7-point band is the price of 4,800 visitors, and it should appear wherever the 6.5% figure is quoted: a funnel plan that needs 7% to hit target is not supported by this data, and one that needs 6% is not refuted either. The normal approximation is fine here (312 events is plenty). For small counts — a page with 11 conversions — the normal interval misbehaves, even dipping below zero, and an exact or Wilson interval should be used instead. The deeper point: a rate without its interval is a rumor; the interval is what makes it a measurement.

A checkout test shows control abandonment 612/1,500 and variant 548/1,520. A PM reports 'abandonment down 10.5%.' Verify the relative change, compute the absolute difference with its 95% CI, and comment.

Control abandonment is 0.408 and variant is 0.361, so the relative reduction is 0.116 — the PM's 10.5% is roughly right as a relative figure (it computes to about 11.6% here; check their rounding and base). The absolute difference is −4.7 points with 95% CI (-0.0821, -0.0128): the interval excludes zero, so a real improvement is supported, but the true absolute effect could be as small as 1.3 points. Relative percentages on unstated bases are the oldest trick in readout decks: 'down 11.6%' sounds triple the size of 'down 4.7 points,' and on a smaller base the same trick inflates further. Readouts should always carry the two raw rates, the absolute difference, and its interval; the relative number may come along, labeled, after those.

A team ran a test with 3,000 users per group on a metric with baseline 20% and wants to know the minimum detectable effect they actually had at 80% power. Compute the MDE using (1.96 + 0.84) × SE with both groups at p = 0.20.

With p = 0.20 in both groups, the standard error of the difference is 0.0103, and the minimum detectable effect at 80% power is 2.80 × SE = 0.0289 — about 2.9 percentage points, a 14.5% relative lift. Translation: this test was only ever capable of reliably catching effects of 3 points or more. If the result came back '+1.2 points, not significant,' that outcome is nearly uninformative — the design could not have seen a 1.2-point effect even if it were real. Post-hoc MDE is the honest way to report an underpowered null: 'no detectable effect; the test could only rule out effects larger than ~3 points.' The fix list is structural: more traffic, a less noisy metric, variance reduction from pre-period data (CUPED), or accepting a larger MDE because only large effects would change the decision anyway. That last option is legitimate — power should be sized to the decision, not to vanity.

A ratio metric — revenue per session — is tested. Control: total revenue $182,400 over 29,500 sessions; variant: $191,250 over 30,100 sessions. Sessions are the randomization unit. Compute revenue per session in each group and the percent difference. Then, given the per-session revenue sd is $26 in both groups, compute the 95% CI for the difference.

Revenue per session is 6.183 control vs 6.354 variant, a difference of 0.0276 in relative terms — about +2.8%. With per-session sd of $26, the standard error of the difference is 0.213 and the 95% interval is (-0.247, 0.588) dollars — it includes zero, so the +2.8% headline is not established. Ratio metrics mislead teams in two specific ways. First, dividing aggregates hides the unit-level variance; the CI must be built from session-level data (or a delta-method/bootstrap equivalent), never from the two totals alone. Second, a ratio can rise because the denominator fell — if the variant drove away low-value sessions, revenue per session improves while total revenue rots; always read the numerator and denominator beside the ratio. Here totals did rise, so the story is coherent, just not yet proven at this sample size.

Explain sample ratio mismatch (SRM): a test designed 50/50 with 201,400 users total shows 102,900 in control and 98,500 in variant. Compute the chi-square statistic for the split and say what an SRM usually means and what to do.

Under a true 50/50 split the expected count is 100,700 per group; the chi-square statistic is 96.1 on one degree of freedom — astronomically beyond the 3.84 threshold for 5% or even the 10.8 for 0.1%. A split this lopsided is not bad luck; it is evidence the randomization or logging pipeline is broken: a bot filter eating one arm, a redirect that drops variant users, a bucketing bug, differential tracking failure. The crucial point is that SRM invalidates the readout even if the metric difference looks clean, because whatever ate 4,400 variant users almost certainly did not eat them at random — it preferentially removed some kind of user, biasing the comparison in an unknown direction. The protocol is: stop, do not 'adjust for it,' find the mechanism, fix it, rerun. Teams that ship through an SRM because the result agreed with their hopes are reading tea leaves with extra steps.
An email test: control click rate 2.31% on 38,000 sends; variant 2.58% on 37,500 sends. Compute the z-statistic for the difference and the two-sided conclusion at 5%.

The difference is 0.0027 (0.27 points) with SE 0.00112, giving z = 2.40 — significant at the 5% level, with room to spare. But significance is the beginning of the readout, not the end. A 0.27-point click lift on a 2.31% base is an 11.7% relative gain in clicks; whether it matters depends on what clicks are worth downstream, and click lifts from subject-line curiosity routinely fail to convert into orders. The responsible readout: 'clicks up, z = 2.4; downstream order rate per send unchanged within noise; ship the subject line if the change is free, but do not book revenue from it.' Also note the denominator discipline: rates here are per send; if variant sends bounced less, part of the 'lift' is deliverability, not persuasion. Check the funnel stage by stage before crediting the copy.

A signup flow test has only reached 900 users per group with baseline conversion 12%. The PM asks for 'a quick significance check.' Compute the standard error of the difference at the null and explain what differences are even visible at this size.

At the null the standard error is 0.0153, so an observed difference needs to exceed about 0.0300 — 3 points, a 25% relative swing — just to reach nominal significance, and to have had 80% power the true effect would need to be near 4.3 points. In plain terms, at 900 per group the test can only 'see' enormous effects; a realistic 1-point improvement will read as noise whichever way it lands. Running the check anyway invites the worst outcome: a random +3.1-point wobble gets declared a win and shipped. The honest answer to the PM is the required sample for the effect they care about — for a 1.5-point lift at 80% power, roughly 7,900 per group — and a decision about whether the traffic or the patience exists. If neither exists, a qualitative usability study will teach more than this test can.

A test reports variant better on the primary metric but the team sliced by 14 segments and found 'new users on Android in Canada' significantly worse. If all 14 segment tests are run at 5% on a true null, what is the probability at least one shows a false significant result? What should the team do with the Canada finding?

With 14 independent looks at a null effect, the chance of at least one false alarm is 1 − 0.95^14 = 0.512 — a coin flip. So a single 'significant' segment among fourteen is close to the expected background rate of noise, and slicing by three dimensions at once (new × Android × Canada) makes the cell small and its variance huge on top of the multiplicity. The correct treatment: label it a hypothesis, not a finding. If the segment matters strategically, run a confirmatory test powered for that segment, or check whether the effect replicates in the next test's data. What not to do is carve Canada-Android-new-users out of the launch on this evidence — that is how roadmaps fill with ghosts. Pre-declaring the two or three segments that will be examined, before data arrives, is the discipline that keeps segment analysis honest; everything else is exploration and should be priced as such.
A retention test: 30-day retention is 41.2% (n = 2,050) control and 44.0% (n = 2,010) variant. Compute the 95% CI for the difference and state whether the team can claim a retention win.

The difference is 0.028 (2.8 points) with SE 0.0155; the 95% interval is (-0.0024, 0.0584). It just barely includes zero (the lower bound is a hair below it), so the strict claim 'we improved retention' is not supported at the 5% level — z ≈ 1.80, p ≈ 0.07. The honest readout language matters: 'directionally positive, not yet conclusive; extending the test two more weeks would resolve it' is accurate, while both 'no effect' and 'retention win' overclaim in opposite directions. Retention tests have a second trap: the variant cohort is younger in exposure terms if assignment was staggered, and day-30 windows measured at different calendar times import seasonality. Before extending, verify both cohorts' day-30 windows cover the same calendar mix. If extending is impossible, a decision to ship can still be right — but it should be logged as a judgment call under uncertainty, not as a measured win.

A team wants to detect a 0.2-point lift on a 1.1% base conversion (a push-notification change). Compute the required sample per group at 80% power, 5% two-sided, and comment on feasibility if daily traffic is 60,000 users total.

The requirement is 46472 users per group — about 46,000 — or 1.5 days of the entire site's traffic split two ways. Feasible here, barely, but look at what the arithmetic is saying: an 18% relative lift on a rare event still needs six figures of users because the signal (0.2 points) is small against Bernoulli noise at p ≈ 0.01. Rare-event metrics are the most expensive measurements in the building. The alternatives deserve airtime before committing the traffic: test the notification on a higher-frequency proxy (opens within an hour) while treating conversion as a guardrail; enrich the sample with the segment that actually receives pushes; or accept that some small-base questions are answered by judgment plus monitoring rather than by experiment. Also note the asymmetry of regret: a push change is cheap to reverse, so the cost of a wrong ship is low — the power requirement should reflect that, and an 80%-power, two-week test may be over-engineering for a reversible tweak.

A founder says: 'The test was significant, p = 0.03, so there's a 97% chance the variant is better.' Correct the misreading precisely, and give the plain-language statement the data does support, using a hypothetical observed lift of +0.8 points with 95% CI (+0.1, +1.5).

The p-value is not the probability the variant is better. p = 0.03 means: if the variant did nothing at all, data this extreme or more would still show up 3% of the time by chance. It is a statement about the data under a hypothetical null, not a probability over hypotheses — computing 'the chance the variant is better' requires a prior and a Bayesian calculation, which nobody ran. What the data do support, in plain language: 'We observed +0.8 points; the 95% confidence interval is +0.1 to +1.5 points, so effects from barely-positive to solidly positive are all consistent with what we saw; effects of zero or less are not, at this confidence level.' Note the interval also disciplines enthusiasm: the most likely true value is not automatically +0.8, and planning revenue on the top of the interval (+1.5) is as unjustified as the founder's 97%. If the decision needs a probability — 'chance this beats the rollout cost' — that is a legitimate Bayesian question; it just has to be computed as one, with the prior on the table.

Summarize this readout as a small table: three tests ended this week. Test A: n = 24,000/group, diff +1.01 points, SE 0.40. Test B: n = 1,900/group, diff +2.9 points, SE 1.85. Test C: n = 9,800/group, diff −0.35 points, SE 0.30. For each, give z and the 95% CI, then a one-line verdict per test.

| Test | Diff (pts) | z | 95% CI | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | +1.01 | 2.52 | (0.23, 1.79) | Ship: interval entirely positive |
| B | +2.90 | 1.57 | (-0.73, 6.53) | Biggest point estimate, weakest evidence: interval spans harm to large gain; rerun bigger |
| C | −0.35 | -1.17 | (-0.94, 0.24) | No effect established; interval rules out large gains, small harm possible |

The teaching point of the week is Test B: the largest headline number carries the least information, because its sample is a twelfth of A's. Ranking tests by point estimate instead of by interval is how portfolios fill with loud noise. Test C deserves equal care in the opposite direction — 'not significant' does not mean 'zero'; it means the truth is somewhere in a band that includes a small real loss, which matters if the change also costs money to maintain.

A marketplace tests a new ranking: orders per visitor rise from 0.184 to 0.197, with 41,000 visitors per group. Treating orders per visitor as a proportion-like rate with variance p(1−p) is wrong because some visitors order twice; the measured sd of orders per visitor is 0.51 in both groups. Compute the SE and CI properly with the measured sd.

Using the measured per-visitor standard deviation, the standard error of the difference is 0.00356 and the 95% interval for the +0.013 difference is (0.0060, 0.0200) — clearly positive. Had the team used the Bernoulli variance p(1−p) ≈ 0.15 (sd ≈ 0.39), they would have understated the standard error by about 24% and overstated their certainty, because repeat orders inflate the true variance (sd 0.51) beyond the binary formula. This is the general rule for count and revenue metrics: the variance must come from the unit-level data, not from a formula borrowed from coin flips. The same trap appears with clustered data — orders per account, messages per user — wherever one unit contributes multiple events. When in doubt, compute the empirical sd of the per-unit metric and, if the distribution is heavy-tailed, confirm with a bootstrap before booking the win.
A pump has a constant failure rate of 0.0008 per hour. What is its MTBF, and what is the probability it survives a 720-hour month of continuous operation?

MTBF = 1/λ = 1250 hours. Under the exponential model, survival over 720 hours is R = exp(−λt) = exp(−0.576) = 0.562 — about a 56% chance of a failure-free month, or 44% chance of at least one failure. That pairing surprises people: a component whose mean life is nearly two months still fails in almost half of all single months, because the exponential distribution is wide — its standard deviation equals its mean. Planning maintenance off MTBF alone ('it lasts 1,250 hours, the month is only 720') is the classic error; reliability is a probability statement about a mission duration, not a promise. The constant-rate assumption fits mid-life electronic and mechanical wear items poorly at the edges: new pumps fail early (installation defects) and old ones wear out, both of which the single λ hides.

A server's disk subsystem: one disk has a 0.92 probability of surviving the year. The server mirrors two independent disks (data lost only if both fail within the rebuild window — ignore rebuild risk). What is the probability the mirrored pair survives the year, versus a striped pair where either failure loses data?

Mirroring: data survives unless both disks die, probability (0.08)² = 0.0064, so survival is 0.9936 — 99.36%. Striping inverts the logic: the volume survives only if both disks survive, 0.92² = 0.8464 — 84.6%, worse than a single disk. Same hardware, opposite reliability, purely from the failure logic. The independence assumption is where the mirror's promise can crack: disks from the same manufacturing batch, in the same thermal environment, on the same power supply, fail together more often than (0.08)² suggests, and the ignored rebuild window is precisely when the surviving disk is stressed hardest and a second failure is most likely. Real array design therefore treats the computed 99.36% as an upper bound and attacks the common causes — batch diversity, cooling, scrubbing — that the simple product rule cannot see.

A production line needs all four stations up: their reliabilities over a shift are 0.98, 0.96, 0.99, and 0.94. What is the line's reliability over a shift, and which station should engineering attack first?

Series reliability multiplies: 0.8755 — the line completes only about 87.5% of shifts without a station failure, even though every individual station is 94% or better. Four good components in series make a mediocre system; twenty would make a bad one. The weakest station (0.94) is the first target, and the math backs the instinct precisely: raising it to 0.97 lifts the line to about 90.3%, while perfecting the 0.99 station to 1.00 gains less than one point. Marginal analysis, not averages, should rank the work — the derivative of system reliability with respect to each component is the product of all the others, so the smallest factor always offers the largest leverage per point gained. The model assumes stations fail independently; a shared cause like plant air pressure or a power dip would make the true figure worse than 87.5%.

Fleet data: 214 pumps accumulated 1,870,000 operating hours last year with 96 failures. Estimate the failure rate per hour and per 1,000 hours, the implied MTBF, and the expected failures next year if the fleet runs 1,950,000 hours.

The estimated failure rate is λ = 5.13e-05 per hour, i.e. 0.051 failures per 1,000 operating hours, implying an MTBF of 19479 hours. At next year's planned exposure, expected failures are 100.1 — budget and spares should be planned around roughly 100 failures, with Poisson spread of about ±10 (one sd is √100). Two honesty notes. First, this estimate pools all pumps as identical; if the fleet mixes ages, the pooled rate describes no actual pump, and the oldest quartile is probably failing at several times the pooled rate — stratify by age before ordering spares. Second, the estimate's own uncertainty: 96 events give a relative standard error of 1/√96 ≈ 10%, so the 'expected 100' carries a confidence band of roughly 82–120. Point estimates from failure counts always deserve that band in the report.
A drone needs at least 3 of its 4 motors working to stay airborne. Each motor has reliability 0.97 over a flight. Compute the probability the drone stays airborne, and compare with needing all 4.

P(at least 3 of 4) = C(4,3)·0.97³·0.03 + 0.97⁴ = 0.9948 — about 99.48%. Needing all four gives 0.8853, 88.5%. Tolerating one failure buys nearly eleven points of mission reliability from identical motors; that is the power of k-out-of-n redundancy, and it is why multirotor design accepts the weight of extra motors. The binomial calculation assumes independent motor failures — the assumption to interrogate, because the realistic killers are common-cause: a battery sag under load, a firmware bug, or a propeller batch defect takes all four together and the 99.48% evaporates. Redundancy math prices only the independent part of risk. A sound reliability case therefore pairs this number with a common-cause analysis; reporting the binomial figure alone overstates safety in exactly the scenarios that make the news.

Explain the bathtub curve to a facilities manager, and compute what a constant hazard of 0.002 per month implies for 3-year survival of an LED driver fleet, contrasting it with what wear-out would do.

The bathtub curve says hazard is not constant over a product's life: it starts high (infant mortality — manufacturing defects and installation errors kill early), settles into a low flat bottom (random failures during useful life), then rises at the end (wear-out). If the flat-bottom hazard of 0.002 per month held for the whole 36 months, survival would be exp(−0.002×36) = 0.931, about 93%. But that number is only the middle of the bathtub talking. In year one, infant mortality makes real survival worse than the flat model; beyond the driver's rated life, wear-out makes the hazard climb, so extrapolating the flat 0.002 into years 5–8 overstates survival badly. The management translation: budget early replacements for the infant failures (and keep warranty paperwork), plan a proactive fleet swap near rated life rather than running to failure, and never sign a maintenance contract priced off the flat-bottom rate alone — it underprices both ends of the curve.

A service has MTBF of 2,200 hours and mean time to repair of 6.5 hours. Compute steady-state availability and the expected downtime hours per year. The business wants 'three nines' (99.9%) — are they there?

Availability = MTBF/(MTBF + MTTR) = 0.99705 — 99.705%, which is 'two and a half nines' territory, not three. Expected downtime is 25.8 hours per year against a three-nines allowance of 8.76 hours — they are over budget by about a factor of three. The formula also shows the two levers and their asymmetry: halving repair time to 3.25 hours gains as much as doubling MTBF to 4,400, and repair time is usually the cheaper lever (runbooks, spares on site, automated failover). One definitional trap to police: availability claims often quietly exclude planned maintenance and 'partial degradation.' The number above counts everything as either up or down; if the business's three-nines promise is contractual, the exclusions in the contract matter more than the arithmetic.

A component follows a Weibull wear-out model with shape β = 2.2 and characteristic life η = 5,000 hours. Compute reliability at 2,000 hours and at 6,000 hours, and the failure probability by 2,000 hours.

With β = 2.2 > 1 the hazard rises with age — genuine wear-out. R(2000) = exp(−(0.4)^2.2) = 0.875, so the failure probability by 2,000 hours is 0.125, about 12.6%. By 6,000 hours — only 20% past characteristic life — reliability falls to 0.225: more than half the population has failed, because with β = 2.2 failures concentrate around η rather than spreading exponentially. This concentration is operationally convenient: it makes preventive replacement at a fixed age (at 4,000 hours R ≈ 0.54, so replacing there trades a known cost against a population already half-failed) genuinely effective, unlike the exponential case where replacing a healthy old part buys nothing. The caution is parameter honesty: β and η fitted from censored field data carry wide intervals, and a β estimated at 2.2 could be 1.6 — which changes R(6000) substantially. Report the fit's uncertainty with the curve.

A backup generator fails to start on demand with probability 0.03, based on 9 failures in 300 monthly tests. Give the estimate's standard error and 95% CI, and say how many tests would be needed to halve the interval width.

The estimate is 0.030 with standard error 0.0098, giving a 95% interval of (0.0107, 0.0493) — the true fail-to-start probability could plausibly be anywhere from about 1.1% to 4.9%. That width matters because a compliance threshold of, say, 2% sits inside the interval: 300 tests cannot certify this generator either way. Halving the interval width requires four times the data — 1,200 tests — since width shrinks with √n; at monthly testing that is a century, which forces the real answer: pool data across the generator fleet, test more often, or accept a Bayesian estimate borrowing strength from manufacturer data. Rare-event probabilities are brutally expensive to pin down with direct observation, and any report quoting '3%' from 300 trials without the interval is pretending otherwise.
A call-center headset fleet: 1,150 headsets in service, 23 failed this month. Estimate the monthly failure probability per headset and the expected failures next month if the fleet grows to 1,300.

The monthly failure probability per headset is 0.020 — 2% — and at 1,300 headsets the expected failures next month are 26, so spares and the swap-out bench should be stocked for roughly 26 failures, with normal Poisson/binomial wobble of about ±5. Two qualifications before purchasing acts on it. First, the 2% is an average over a mixed-age fleet; if failures concentrate in the oldest cohort, the growing fleet's new headsets will pull the realized rate below 2% — good news, but it means last month's rate overstates next month's need. Second, a single month's count of 23 has a relative standard error near 1/√23 ≈ 21%, so the true monthly rate could reasonably be 1.6–2.4%. For a cheap, swappable item like a headset, planning at the point estimate plus a small buffer is fine; the discipline matters more as unit cost rises.

A vendor advertises a component with 'MTBF 500,000 hours' and a buyer concludes none will fail in their 3-year deployment of 400 units running continuously. Compute the expected number of failures and the probability of zero failures under the exponential model, and correct the conclusion.

MTBF is a population rate, not a lifetime guarantee. Total exposure is 400 × 3 × 8,760 ≈ 10.5 million unit-hours; at one failure per 500,000 hours the expected number of failures is 21.0 — about twenty-one. The probability of zero failures is exp(−21) = 7.40e-10, effectively nil. The buyer confused 'mean time between failures' for a single unit's clock with a promise; in fact a single unit's chance of failing within one MTBF is 1 − exp(−1) ≈ 63%. Vendor MTBF figures also deserve a sourcing question: many are calculated from parts-count prediction handbooks rather than observed in the field, and can be optimistic by an order of magnitude for real environments. The correct procurement ask is the failure rate under stated conditions, the data behind it, and a spares plan sized from the exposure math above — which, at 21 expected failures, argues for roughly two dozen spares or a repair contract, not zero.

Two independent network paths each have availability 0.97 over a month. Traffic survives if either path is up. Compute combined availability and expected downtime minutes per month (30 days), versus a single path.

Parallel availability is 1 − (0.03)² = 0.9991, cutting expected downtime from 1296 minutes a month (about 21.6 hours) on one path to 38.9 minutes. Redundancy's leverage is quadratic on the unavailability: each independent path multiplies the downtime fraction. The word doing the heavy lifting is 'independent.' If both paths share a conduit, a provider's backbone, or a power feed, the joint failure probability is far above 0.0009 and the real availability lands closer to the single-path figure. Diversity audits — physical route maps, provider wholesale relationships, shared building entries — are what turn this arithmetic into reality. Also note availability is not performance: a month can score 99.91% while every failure landed in the busiest hour. Pair the availability target with a worst-hour or traffic-weighted measure before signing an SLA on it.

A safety system uses 2-out-of-3 voting sensors, each with reliability 0.93 per demand, independent. Compute system reliability per demand. Then compute it if a common-cause failure mode with probability 0.02 disables all three together.

Independent case: P(at least 2 of 3 work) = 3·0.93²·0.07 + 0.93³ = 0.9860 — about 98.6%, a solid gain over a single sensor's 93%. Now add a 2% common-cause mode that kills all three at once: system reliability becomes (1 − 0.02) × 0.9860 = 0.9663 — about 96.6%. The common cause, though 'only' 2%, eats more than a third of the redundancy gain, and if it were 5% it would cap the system near 93.6% no matter how many sensors are added. This is the central lesson of safety-system design: past a point, reliability is bought by attacking shared causes — diverse sensor technologies, separated wiring, independent power — not by piling on identical channels. Voting logic also has a second face the calculation omits: spurious trips. A 2oo3 system that shuts the plant down on false alarms trains operators to bypass it, which is a human-factors failure no binomial will show.
A software service's errors arrive as a Poisson process at 2.7 per hour during a launch. What is the probability of an error-free hour, and of more than 5 errors in an hour?

P(0 errors) = exp(−2.7) = 0.067 — only about 7% of launch hours will be clean, so a clean hour is no evidence the rate improved. P(more than 5) = 0.057: roughly 5.7% of hours will look alarming purely by chance, which across a 12-hour launch day means a better-than-even chance of at least one 'spike' that is just Poisson weather. The operational discipline this imposes: judge the launch on the cumulative rate over hours, not on individual hourly counts, and set alert thresholds from the distribution (e.g., alert at 8+, where the tail is ~0.6%) rather than from vibes. The Poisson assumption itself needs watching — real error processes are contagious (one bad deploy raises the rate for hours), so if the observed variance across hours exceeds the mean, the process is overdispersed and these tail numbers understate the extremes.
A manufacturer tests 60 units for 1,000 hours each with 3 failures total. Estimate the failure rate and MTBF under the exponential assumption, and state the total unit-hours behind the estimate.

Total exposure is 60,000 unit-hours. With 3 failures, λ̂ = 5.00e-05 per hour and MTBF = 20000 hours. Report those with their uncertainty or do not report them at all: with only 3 events, the relative standard error of λ̂ is 1/√3 ≈ 58%, so the true MTBF could plausibly be anywhere from roughly 8,000 to over 60,000 hours. This is the chronic weakness of reliability demonstration tests — passing a test with a handful of failures certifies far less than the point estimate suggests, which is why formal demonstration plans specify the test length from the required confidence bound, not from the hoped-for MTBF. Also flag the censoring subtlety: 57 units were still running at 1,000 hours; their unobserved remaining life is exactly what the exponential assumption fills in, so if the failure mode is actually wear-out (rising hazard), this test design would miss it entirely and the MTBF would be optimistic.

Present a small reliability comparison table for a hospital's three backup options for a monitoring system over a 24-hour mission: (a) single unit R = 0.90; (b) two units in parallel, either suffices; (c) two units in series (both needed for full function). Include expected failures per 100 missions for each.

| Configuration | Mission reliability | Expected failures per 100 missions |
|---|---|---|
| Single unit | 0.900 | 10 |
| Two in parallel (either suffices) | 0.990 | 1.0 |
| Two in series (both needed) | 0.810 | 19 |

The same two boxes produce a 0.99 or a 0.81 system depending only on the failure logic — architecture is a reliability decision before any component is chosen. For a monitoring system the parallel option's catch is switchover: the computed 0.990 assumes the backup detects the failure and takes over perfectly; real failover mechanisms have their own failure probability, which belongs in the model as a series element. In a hospital the table also is not the whole decision — a degraded-mode question sits underneath it: if one unit fails mid-mission, does the survivor cover all beds or only critical ones? Reliability numbers should always be quoted against a stated mission definition like that, or the decimals are theater.

An aircraft component's hazard is modeled as constant λ = 1.2e-5 per flight hour. A fleet flies 850,000 hours per year. Compute expected failures per year and the probability that a given airframe (flying 3,100 hours/year) has zero failures of this component in a year.

Fleet-wide, expected failures are 10.2 per year — this component will fail about ten times a year across the fleet, a routine maintenance planning number. For one airframe, the expected count is 1.2e-5 × 3,100 = 0.0372, so P(zero) = 0.963: each airframe has a 96.3% chance of a clean year. Both views are true simultaneously, and confusing them causes real arguments — line mechanics experience the fleet rate ('this part fails all the time') while each aircraft's record looks clean. The constant-hazard assumption is the standard mid-life model; for a component with a known wear mechanism the hazard should be modeled rising with hours since overhaul, and the per-airframe probability should use that airframe's position in the overhaul cycle, not the fleet-average λ. Spares provisioning, though, correctly works off the fleet figure: stock for ~10 events a year, plus Poisson headroom.
A survey of 1,100 voters finds 54% favoring a measure. Compute the 95% margin of error and the confidence interval, and state what the margin does and does not cover.

The standard error is 0.0150, so the margin of error is ±0.029 — about 3 points — and the interval is (0.511, 0.569). Headline translation: support is somewhere in the low-to-high 50s; '54%' alone overstates what 1,100 interviews can know. What the margin covers is only sampling randomness under the design — who happened to be picked. What it does not cover is everything that actually ruins polls: nonresponse bias (who refuses), likely-voter modeling, question wording, and late movement. A poll can be a perfect random sample of the wrong population and carry a tiny margin of error around a wrong number. When comparing two candidates in the same poll, also remember the margin for the gap is larger than the margin for each share — roughly √2 times if the shares were independent, and the correct paired calculation is its own exercise.

A city of 28,000 households wants to estimate support for a recycling program within ±2.5 points at 95% confidence, worst-case p = 0.5. Compute the required sample with and without the finite population correction.

Ignoring the finite population, n₀ = 1.96² × 0.25 / 0.025² = 1537. Applying the finite population correction for N = 28,000 gives n = 1457 — the correction saves about 80 interviews, roughly 5%, because the sample is a noticeable fraction of the city. The worst-case p = 0.5 choice is deliberate insurance: if true support is 70/30, the needed n drops by about 16%, but designing to a guessed p risks an underpowered survey when the guess is wrong. Two practical notes: the ±2.5 points applies to the citywide figure only — any subgroup (a single district) will carry a much wider margin, which should be said in the report before someone quotes a district number. And the computed n is completed interviews; with a 25% response rate the city must invite four times as many households, and the nonrespondents are a bias risk no sample size fixes.

A quality team samples 400 units from a production run of 2,000 and finds 18 defective. Estimate the defect rate with a 95% CI, applying the finite population correction since the sample is 20% of the run.

The sample defect rate is 0.045 (4.5%). With the finite population correction factor √((2000−400)/1999) ≈ 0.895, the standard error is 0.0093 and the interval is (0.0268, 0.0632) — the run's true defect rate is plausibly 2.7% to 6.3%. Sampling a fifth of the run buys real precision: without the correction the interval would be about 12% wider. Whether this triggers a 100% inspection depends on the decision rule set in advance — if the contract rejects runs above 5%, this sample cannot clear the run, because 5% sits inside the interval; it also cannot condemn it. That in-between verdict is a legitimate outcome and the sampling plan should have specified the follow-up (a second, larger sample) before anyone saw the 18. Deciding the next step after seeing data, under pressure from both production and the customer, is how sampling plans quietly become negotiations.

A poll of 800 people reports a subgroup result — voters under 30, n = 96 — as '62% ± 3%.' The ±3% was the full-sample margin. Compute the subgroup's actual margin of error at p = 0.62 and explain the error in the report.

The subgroup's own margin is 1.96 × √(0.62 × 0.38 / 96) = ±0.097 — about ±9.7 points, more than three times the quoted figure. The report committed the most common error in survey journalism: attaching the full-sample margin to every number in the release. Margin of error scales with 1/√n of the group actually being described, and subgroups are small by definition. At n = 96 the honest statement is '62% ± 10,' an interval so wide it supports almost no headline — which is exactly why the error matters: the false precision manufactures a story about young voters that the data cannot carry. The same trap applies to differences between subgroups, whose margins are larger still. A newsroom rule that fixes most of it: never print a subgroup percentage without its own n beside it, and let the n embarrass the claim when it should.

A researcher estimates mean household water use. A pilot gives sd = 41 gallons/day. They want the mean within ±3 gallons at 95% confidence. Compute the required sample size, and the cost implication if each interview costs $28 and the budget is $15,000.

For a mean, n = (1.96σ/E)² = 718 households. At $28 each that is 20091 dollars — about $20,100, over the $15,000 budget. The budget affords 536 interviews, at which the achievable margin is ±3.5 gallons. So the real deliverable is a choice, stated plainly: ±3 gallons for $20k, or ±3.5 gallons for $15k — precision is a purchasable commodity with a √ price curve, and the last increment is always the most expensive because n grows with 1/E². One more caveat: the pilot sd of 41 came from a small pilot and is itself uncertain; prudent design inflates it somewhat (using, say, the pilot's upper confidence bound), because a survey sized on an optimistic σ delivers a wider margin than promised and nobody can retroactively buy the missing interviews.

Two independent polls a week apart: Poll 1 (n = 1,200) has a candidate at 47%, Poll 2 (n = 1,050) has her at 51%. A headline says 'Candidate surges 4 points.' Compute the standard error of the change and assess the headline.

The standard error of the difference between two independent polls is 0.0211, so the 4-point gap is z = 1.89 — well short of significance; the margin of error on the change is ±0.041, about ±4.1 points. The 'surge' is indistinguishable from sampling noise: two polls of a perfectly static race would show a gap this large roughly 6–7% of the time... more precisely, |z| this big occurs about 7% of the time two-sided — uncommon but hardly a headline-grade event, and that is before house effects (different pollsters' methods differ systematically by more than this). The durable rule: a change between polls must be judged against the margin of the difference, which is roughly 1.4× each poll's own margin — never against a single poll's margin, and never by eyeballing whether the two intervals overlap. If the race truly matters, aggregate several polls; averaging shrinks the noise that single-poll headlines feed on.

A health survey uses cluster sampling: 40 clinics, 25 patients each (n = 1,000). The intraclass correlation for the outcome is 0.04. Compute the design effect and the effective sample size, and the margin of error for a proportion at p = 0.5 compared with simple random sampling.

The design effect is 1 + (m − 1)ρ = 1.96: patients within a clinic resemble each other (same staff, same neighborhood), so each additional patient in the same clinic adds less than a full independent observation. The effective sample size is 510, not 1,000, and the margin of error at p = 0.5 is ±0.043 instead of the ±0.031 a simple random sample of 1,000 would give. Ignoring clustering is one of the most consequential quiet errors in applied work: the nominal n flatters every interval in the report by about 40% here. The design lever is the cluster count, not the cluster size — 80 clinics × 12 patients (same budget of interviews, more travel) would cut the design effect to about 1.44 and recover much of the lost precision. When reading any survey, the methods line 'clustered by clinic' should trigger an immediate hunt for the design effect; if it is not reported, assume the intervals are too narrow.

A university surveys alumni satisfaction. Stratified sampling: 60% of alumni are undergrad-only (stratum satisfaction 71%, n sampled 500) and 40% hold graduate degrees (satisfaction 64%, n sampled 500). Compute the correct population estimate and the naive unweighted average, and quantify the bias from ignoring strata weights.

The population estimate must weight by population shares: 0.6 × 0.71 + 0.4 × 0.64 = 0.682 — 68.2%. The naive average of the two stratum numbers is 0.675, overstating satisfaction by -0.007, about 0.7 points, because the sample deliberately over-represents graduate alumni (50% of sample vs 40% of population) and they are the less satisfied stratum. Oversampling a stratum is good design — it buys precision for that group — but the weights must be repaid at analysis time.
